texts.preamble: State Of M.P. vs Dinesh Singh on 25 June, 2025 Author: Anil Verma Bench: Anil Verma Neutral Citation No. 2025:Mphc-Gwl:12809 1 In The High Court Of Madhya Pradesh At Gwalior Before Hon'Ble Shri Justice Anil Verma On The 25th Of June, 2025 Criminal Appeal No. 303 of 2006 State Of M.P. Versus Dinesh Singh Appearance: Shri Harish Sharma - Public Prosecutor for the appella None for the respondent. Order Appellant has preferred this criminal appeal under Section 378 of Cr.P.C. after obtaining leave vide order dated 17.4.2006 from this Court under Section 378(4) of Cr.P.C. against the impugned judgment of acquittal dated 3.1.2005 passed by Judicial Magistrate First Class, Vidisha in Criminal Case No.148/2004 for offence under Sections 16(1)(a)(i)(ii) of Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 (in short PFA Act). 2.
texts.facts: Order Appellant has preferred this criminal appeal under Section 378 of Cr.P.C. after obtaining leave vide order dated 17.4.2006 from this Court under Section 378(4) of Cr.P.C. against the impugned judgment of acquittal dated 3.1.2005 passed by Judicial Magistrate First Class, Vidisha in Criminal Case No.148/2004 for offence under Sections 16(1)(a)(i)(ii) of Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 (in short PFA Act). 2. As per prosecution story on 15.5.1998 Food Inspector Ram Singh along with S.N. Verma inspected the Shreshti Sweets and found that the respondent was selling several sweets along with curd. Food Inspector disclosed his identity, gave notice to the respondent/accused and purchased 600 Gm. curd after paying Rs.12.50. He disclosed that the sample would be sent for analysis. Food Inspector divided the sample into three equal parts and added 48 drops of formalin in each part and kept the sample in dry and NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2025:MPHC-GWL:12809 2 CRA-303-2006 clean glass. Bottle was sealed on the spot. The spot map was also prepared. One bottle of the sample was sent to the Public Analyst. Public Analyst found that the same was found adulterated and unfit for human consumption. On receipt of the report of Public Analyst, the Food Inspector obtained sanction. It is also found that respondent/accused was selling the aforesaid product without having any valid license for its trade. Copy of report of analyst was also sent along with the memorandum to the respondent/accused by the registered post at his address in compliance of provision of Section 13(2) of PFA Act and thereafter complaint has been filed before the Trial Court. The Trial Court framed the charges under Section 7(1), 7(5) r/w Section 16(1)(a)(i)(ii) of PFA Act. The appellant abjured his guilt and pleaded complete innocence. 4. Prosecution has examined as many as three witnesses while respondent/accused has examined one defence witness. Being aggrieved by the acquittal of the respondent , appellant has preferred this appeal.
texts.arguments: 6. Learned Pubic Prosecutor for the appellant submits that the Trial Court has not properly appreciated the oral as well as documentary evidence available on record and wrongly acquitted the respondent/accused from the NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2025:MPHC-GWL:12809 3 CRA-303-2006 charges leveled against him. Learned counsel for the respondent/accused before the Trial Court has forcefully contended that in view Section 13 of PFA Act, the report of Public Analyst has become inadmissible in evidence is a just and proper because it is not made clear during the sample process or in the complaint that the curd was made from milk of cow or buffalo. In the case of State of M.P. vs. Arvind Joshi reported in 2008 NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2025:MPHC-GWL:12809 5 CRA-303-2006 (2) Crimes 228 (M.P.), this Court has held as under: "10. 12. In a case of State of Goa vs. Sanjay Thakran and Anr. (2007) 2 SCC (Cri) 162 the Hon. Supreme Court has held that: "While exercising the powers in an appeal against the order of acquittal the court of appeal would not ordinarily interfere with the order of acquittal unless the approach of the lower court is vitiated by some manifest illegality and the conclusion arrived at would not be arrived at by any reasonable person and, therefore, the decision is to be characterized as perverse. Merely because two views are possible, the court of appeal would not take the view, which would upset the judgment delivered by the court below. A duty is cast upon the appellate court, in such circumstances, to re appreciate the evidence to arrive at a just decision on the basis of material placed on record to find out whether any of the accused is connected with State Of M.P. vs Dinesh Singh on 25 June, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/117475600/ 3 commission of the crime he is charged with." 13. In a case of Peerappaand Ors. v. State of Karnataka (2006) 1 SCC (Cri) 586, their Lordships recalled the observations made by His Lordship of the Supreme Court, in a case of Kashiram v. State of M.P. (2002) 1 SCC 71, as observed, thus: "Though the High Court while hearing an appeal against an acquittal has powers as wide and comprehensive as in an appeal against a conviction and while exercising its appellate jurisdiction the High Court can reappraise the evidence, arrive at findings at variance with those recorded by the trial court in its order of acquittal and arrive at its own findings, yet, the salutary principle which would guide the High Court is -if two views are reasonable possible, one supporting the acquittal and the other recording a conviction, the High Court would not interfere merely because it feels that sitting as a trial court its view would have been one of recording a NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2025:MPHC-GWL:12809 6 CRA-303-2006 conviction. It follows as a necessary corollary that it is obligatory on the High Court while reversing an order of acquittal to consider and discuss each of the reasons given by the trial court to acquit the accused and then to dislodge those reasons. . Merely because two views are possible, the High Court would not disturb the finding of acquittal recorded by the Trial Court as held in the decision of State of M.P. Vs. Ramcharan and others, 1985 MPLJ 714. 14.
